name: Black walnut hull hair dye

card.summary: A plant-based brown dye made from the green outer husk of the black walnut, used to tint hair and cover grey with a natural brown tone.
card.aka: Walnut hull dye, walnut husk dye
card.note: Stains skin strongly; no safety testing for hair use located.

quick.overview:
Black walnut hulls are the soft outer husks of Juglone-rich Juglans nigra nuts. Their juice and extracts stain brown, and people have used them as a natural brown dye for fibre and, in some accounts, hair.

For looks, the idea is a do-it-yourself brown tint that darkens hair or blends grey without synthetic dyes. Wikipedia notes that early American settlers reportedly used it for this, giving brownish-black shades, though that claim is flagged as needing a better source.
quick.how: Practitioners soak or simmer the hulls to make a brown liquid, then apply it to hair as a rinse or paste. The shade depends on how dark the hull liquid has become as the husk ages.
quick.risks: The staining compounds mark skin, clothing and surfaces, and juglone is toxic to some plants. No published safety testing of walnut hull dye on human hair or scalp was found; people with tree-nut allergy may wish to take particular care.

lead: Black walnut hull hair dye is a traditional plant-based colorant made from the husks of the black walnut tree, Juglans nigra. The hulls contain juglone, plumbagin and tannins, which stain strongly [1]. As a hair colour, it gives a brown tint and is used by people who want a natural alternative to synthetic dyes or who want to darken grey hair.

Black walnut hulls appear among the plant sources historically used for hair dyeing, alongside henna, indigo and senna [2]. Wikipedia's tree article says early American settlers reportedly used the dye to colour hair, producing brownish-black shades, but the claim carries a request for a better source [1].

chain: Tannins and quinones stain the strands brown
angle.text: Hull extract stains hair brown, so people use it to darken hair or blend grey. The result varies with how the extract is prepared.

paras: The Petersen field guide describes the dye as yellowish-brown, while others report brownish-black; Wikipedia suggests the difference may come from the liquid darkening as the husk turns from light green to black [1]. Walnut tannins can also act as a mordant that helps dye bind to fibre [1].

Plant-based hair dyes date to antiquity, with recipes in the Ebers Papyrus (c. 1550 BCE) and Assyrian tablets, and walnut hulls are among the plants listed in dye histories [2]. Synthetic dyes followed William Henry Perkin's 1856 discovery of mauveine [2].

The staining compounds mark skin and surfaces, and juglone can harm sensitive plants such as tomatoes and apples [1]. Wikipedia's hair colouring article focuses its safety discussion on synthetic dyes, and no safety assessment of walnut hull dye on hair was found in the sources consulted [2].

timeline.event: The Ebers Papyrus records plant-based hair dye recipes [2].
Mauveine, the first synthetic dye, is discovered, beginning the shift to synthetic hair colourants [2].
